_meta.description: Hand-annotated drug records for the patient filter. This is the stand-in for the DrugCentral join that merge.py will supply: enzyme flags, ATC codes, adverse-event terms, formulations, routes, target compartment, and Health Canada DPD status.
_meta.provenance: Enzyme flags follow the FDA CYP1A2 inhibitor/inducer table and the Flockhart P450 table. ATC codes are WHO ATC. Adverse-event terms are label-level facts. Formulation and route entries describe the marketed forms. Fields we could not establish are null, and the matching rule then reports itself as not enforced rather than silently passing the drug.
_meta.estimates: smallest_tablet_mm values are physical-size estimates, not sourced measurements. They are the only soft numbers in this file; replace them from a product monograph before quoting one to a judge.
_meta.replaced_by: E1's DrugCentral join. The schema is deliberately tolerant so merge.py can hand over a superset of these keys.
_meta.selection: Chosen so that every one of the eight rules fires at least once and at least four drugs clear all eight.

drugs.name: memantine
drugs.notes: NMDA antagonist. Also sits in the graveyard: MND-SMART phase 3, n=554, reported negative in 2024.

drugs.name: baclofen
drugs.notes: Spasticity standard of care in ALS. Expect it to fail the myopathy rule on the 'muscular weakness' term - that is the rule being conservative, and a clinician would overrule it.

drugs.name: rasagiline
drugs.notes: MAO-B inhibitor. Clears all eight rules, and is in the graveyard - the trial_history stage, not the patient filter, is what should catch it.

drugs.name: pyridostigmine
drugs.notes: Quaternary ammonium, so it does not cross. Peripheral target plus BBB-negative is the correct sign - the clean positive case for the signed rule.

drugs.name: ceftriaxone
drugs.notes: The signed barrier rule's headline case. It was taken to an ALS phase 3 on the theory that it raises the glial glutamate transporter EAAT2 in the CNS - a central target - and it is predicted not to cross. Clears the other seven rules and is eliminated on direction alone.

drugs.name: fluvoxamine
drugs.notes: The strongest CYP1A2 inhibitor in clinical use. Fails on rule 1 before anything else is considered.

drugs.name: ciprofloxacin
drugs.notes: A reminder that the filter catches ordinary prescriptions, not just exotic candidates - an antibiotic for a chest infection collides with his riluzole.

drugs.name: carbamazepine
drugs.notes: The induction case. Lowering riluzole exposure is a failure mode people forget to screen for.

drugs.name: mexiletine
drugs.notes: Used off-label for ALS cramps, and it fails three rules at once: CYP1A2 inhibition, capsule-only, and a muscle target with brain penetration.

drugs.name: morphine
drugs.notes: Genuinely used in ALS palliative care. The filter is a screening rule, not a prescribing ban - a palliative decision can overrule it, deliberately and on the record.

drugs.name: diazepam
drugs.notes: Benzodiazepine. Small tablet, liquid available, crosses beautifully - and still disqualified, because the only rule that matters here is his supine FVC.

drugs.name: topiramate
drugs.notes: In the graveyard already, and it would have failed the patient filter on nutrition alone. He is down 8.5 kg.

drugs.name: simvastatin
drugs.notes: The myopathy case, against a CK of 470 U/L.

drugs.name: gabapentin
drugs.notes: Two independent failures: an FDA respiratory-depression warning that names reduced respiratory reserve, and a CNS target it is predicted not to reach. Also in the graveyard from a 2001 phase 3.

drugs.name: salbutamol
drugs.notes: The dexterity case. A 3 kg pinch cannot compress an MDI canister, and his 310 L/min cough peak flow is also marginal for a dry powder device.

drugs.name: interferon beta-1a
drugs.notes: Self-injection he cannot perform, and the barrier model declares it out of domain - so the signed rule correctly refuses to fire on a 22 kDa protein.

drugs.name: tirasemtiv
drugs.notes: The precedent for the signed barrier rule. Fast skeletal muscle troponin activator: a muscle target in a brain-penetrant molecule. VITALITY-ALS (phase 3, reported 2019) missed its slow-vital-capacity endpoint and Cytokinetics rebuilt the mechanism as reldesemtiv.

drugs.name: reldesemtiv
drugs.notes: Tirasemtiv's successor. Same muscle target, intended to stay peripheral, so it passes the signed barrier rule with the correct sign - and still fails the Canada rule, because it was never approved anywhere. It also failed COURAGE-ALS for futility in 2025, which is the honest footnote: getting the delivery direction right does not rescue a mechanism that does not work.

drugs.name: riluzole
drugs.notes: His own drug, as a positive control, annotated as the product he can actually get in Hamilton - Rilutek, Apo-Riluzole or Mylan-Riluzole, all 50 mg tablets. Note the swallow rule fails it, and that is the delivery gap: computed from his chart rather than asserted.

drugs.name: riluzole oral suspension
drugs.notes: Tiglutik in the US (NDA 209080, approved 2018) and Teglutik in Europe: riluzole as a thickened oral suspension, currently marketed, made for ALS patients who cannot swallow tablets. It clears the swallow rule that his tablet fails, then fails the Canada rule - the Health Canada DPD holds only three riluzole products and all three are 50 mg tablets. Same molecule, same dose, one rule apart. See docs/riluzole-delivery-gap.md.

drugs.name: riluzole oral film
drugs.notes: Exservan: a riluzole oral film placed on the tongue, label instruction 'Do not administer with liquids'. FDA-approved 2019-11-22 under NDA 212640, discontinued 2024-09-30, and FDA withdrew the approval on 2025-02-14 (90 FR 3877), so it no longer exists anywhere. It never held a Canadian DIN in any status. Kept in the set as the historical case - the easiest formulation for a patient like Alex was built, then taken off the market. The live comparator is the oral suspension above.
